briefing: Trump named hardline immigration adviser Stephen Miller White House chief of staff after Republicans' heavy midterm losses, while two Senate races remain uncalled. A strong U.S. jobs report (165,000 added) contrasts with Canada's loss of 4,700 jobs and 6.7% unemployment, leaving the Bank of Canada in a tough spot. At home, Ottawa's new budget, Ontario student protests over OSAP and Toronto's looming budget shortfall continue to dominate.
headline: Trump taps Stephen Miller as chief of staff; Canada budget lands

stories.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
stories.summary: Days after heavy Republican midterm losses, Trump said Miller, a lead architect of his immigration crackdown, will take over as chief of staff on Monday, Nov. 9.
stories.now: Trump announced on Truth Social that Stephen Miller will become White House chief of staff on Monday, November 9. Susie Wiles, the first woman to hold the job, is moving to the president's political operation. Asked why, Trump said he "wanted to make a change" and did not explain what had shifted since October, when he said there was "zero chance" he would replace her. Reports link the move to Trump's anger over Tuesday's losses and describe it as a turn further to the right. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become speaker, sharply criticized the choice.
stories.backstory: Wiles ran Trump's 2024 campaign and was named chief of staff after his election win, the first woman in the role. Miller worked in Trump's first-term White House and returned in 2025 as a senior policy adviser focused on immigration and deportations. Republicans lost the House and likely the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, prompting questions about how the White House would respond.

stories.why: The chief of staff controls access to the president and how policy is carried out. Miller's rise signals that the administration may double down on immigration enforcement and confrontation with a Democratic House.
stories.impact: A harder immigration line could affect cross-border travel, work permits and trade talks with Canada. Ontario businesses with U.S. ties should expect continued uncertainty.

stories.backstory: Canada's job market has weakened through the autumn as U.S. tariffs weigh on manufacturing and hiring. The Bank of Canada has raised rates recently and said more hikes were possible, making labour data closely watched. Three straight monthly job losses are unusual outside a downturn.
stories.headline: Canada loses 4,700 jobs in October; unemployment rises to 6.7%
stories.impact: Young workers and job seekers in Ontario face a tougher market. Weak hiring may ease pressure for higher borrowing costs, but job security worries can weigh on household spending and the housing market.
stories.now: Employment fell by 4,700 in October after losses of 68,000 in September and 42,000 in August, while economists had expected a small gain. The unemployment rate rose to 6.7% from 6.5%, the second straight monthly increase. Youth unemployment (ages 15 to 24) rose 0.7 points to 13.7%. Alberta lost 24,000 jobs and its jobless rate reached 7.3%.

stories.backstory: Champagne announced the Nov. 5 date on Oct. 20. The budget arrives while U.S. tariffs remain in place and the Bank of Canada has just raised its rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023.
stories.headline: Carney government's second budget projects $62.3B deficit with $142B in new spending
stories.impact: Watch for small-business tax changes, the deficit figure and immigration targets, which affect GTA hiring, rents and housing demand.
stories.now: The budget projects a $62.3-billion deficit for 2026-27, reported as down from $65.3 billion in the spring forecast, with deficits above $50 billion in each of the next four years. It adds roughly $142.1 billion in new spending over five years, much of it classed as capital spending. Debt interest is projected to reach about $85.5 billion a year by the end of the decade. Commentators are split between those who call it fiscally measured for bond markets and those who say it borrows too much. The Liberals still need opposition support in the House of Commons to pass it. The immigration levels update was expected alongside it; details were not confirmed in this run. Coverage also highlights a plan to end homelessness in Canada within ten years, focused on transitional housing and work with the provinces, and spending meant to strengthen economic and cultural sovereignty, paid for in part by an oil-revenue windfall.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.
stories.headline: Democrats flip Congress; final House and Senate counts still firming up
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.
stories.now: NBC News projects Democrats will win at least 259 of 435 House seats, while CBS News gives a range of 251 to 268. Democrats are also projected to hold at least 54 Senate seats, with the Alaska and Mississippi contests not yet called. Republicans had held the House 218-214 and the Senate 53-47 before the vote. Wins reached into deep-red and battleground states, which analysts read as a rejection of the president's agenda. Final tallies may shift as late ballots are counted. In Mississippi, Democratic and Republican lawyers are trading legal letters over how ballots are counted in the razor-thin Senate race, according to The Guardian.

stories.headline: U.S. adds 165,000 jobs in October, well above forecasts; unemployment 4.1%
stories.summary: A stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report pushed Treasury yields up and raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
stories.now: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far above forecasts of roughly 60,000, and the unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from the expected 4.2%. August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month and 3.1% from a year ago. Weak spots include the average length of unemployment (27.1 weeks, the longest since 2021) and the broader U-6 underemployment rate, which rose to 7.9%.
stories.backstory: The U.S. unemployment rate has stayed between 4.1% and 4.3% since March. Tariffs, high energy prices tied to the Iran war and AI-related hiring have pulled the labour market in different directions. The Fed has been weighing whether inflation requires higher rates.

stories.why: Hot jobs data makes the Fed more likely to raise rates, which moves bond yields and the U.S. dollar and can ripple into Canadian borrowing costs.
stories.impact: Higher U.S. yields can push up Canadian fixed mortgage rates. Canada's weak October jobs report points the other way, so the Bank of Canada faces a tougher call on Dec. 9.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.
stories.headline: Trump says U.S. may have to 'destroy' rest of Iran as war shadows post-midterm politics
stories.impact: Lower crude should show up at GTA pumps within days, but a failed deal could send prices back up. Fuel costs feed into groceries, deliveries and transit.
stories.now: CNBC reports Brent crude rose about 1.6% to US$96.15 a barrel and U.S. crude to US$88.64 on Thursday, after both tumbled more than 8% in the prior session to their lowest since Aug. 31. Traders had bet that Republican losses in Congress lower the risk of escalation. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents after using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz. Eurasia Group trimmed its odds of renewed U.S. strikes to 60% from 65% but cut the odds of a deal to 10% from 20%, warning that escalation could push Brent to US$110–125. Trump has said the U.S. may have to 'destroy' the rest of Iran.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, but the midterms followed a year of tariffs, high gas prices linked to the Iran war and mid-decade redistricting fights in several states. Dozens of House Republicans had announced retirements before the vote.

stories.impact: Canadian businesses will watch whether Congress tries to limit tariffs; any change would come slowly, and existing tariffs stay unless the White House acts.

Democratic leaders have begun laying out an agenda that includes investigations of the administration. Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping aside as House Republican leader, as reported earlier this week.

stories.backstory: Broad Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian counter-tariffs. Separate U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos hit Ontario's factories hardest. Ottawa is courting other partners while talks continue.
stories.headline: Canada-U.S. trade talks continue as Democrats vow to repeal tariffs
stories.impact: Jobs in Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and GTA parts plants stay exposed, and some imports such as paint, carpets and air conditioners may cost more.
stories.now: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday he had a good conversation with Trump and that negotiators will keep working on a deal, but no tariff relief or timeline has been announced. DNC chair Ken Martin said Democrats should repeal Trump's tariffs if they take power after the midterms, citing exit polls showing voters think the country is on the wrong track. On Oct. 30 the U.S. reshuffled its list of Canadian goods facing 50% tariffs. Trump has said steel and auto tariffs on Canada will rise to 50% on Jan. 1. Jean Simard of the Aluminum Association of Canada said the midterm results could mark a turning point for tariff relief. Global News reports Canadian ministers said it would be dangerous to assume relations with the U.S. will shift right away after Democrats won Congress, and that Canada's focus has not changed.

stories.backstory: OSAP is Ontario's student loan and grant program. The province froze aid to career colleges while auditors review how funds were used, and recent changes to the program and tuition rules have sparked campus protests. Students and compliant colleges say the blanket pause hurts those who did nothing wrong.
stories.headline: Thousands of Ontario students walk out over OSAP cuts: 'We can't afford rent'
stories.impact: Students at career colleges may face delays to aid, and others should check their OSAP offer and campus fee notices for the coming terms.
stories.now: Students at campuses across Ontario, including a large walkout at the University of Toronto, protested OSAP cuts and tuition costs on Nov. 5. Separately, Premier Doug Ford said auditors from KPMG are clearing lower-risk career colleges first so their OSAP funding can be unfrozen, but he gave no timeline. Advanced Education Minister Nolan Quinn has said the pause lasts until a stronger approval process is in place, which he expects in the new year. Preliminary audit findings raised concerns about student verification and have been referred to the OPP, and Career Colleges Ontario wants access restored without delay.

stories.backstory: In 2023 Toronto faced a large budget hole. Ford and Chow agreed a package that included the province taking over the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway, with roughly $1.2 billion over three years. That deal is now winding down, and the city has been seeking more help.
stories.headline: With a $1.12-billion budget shortfall looming, Ford rules out a 'new deal' 2.0 for Toronto
stories.impact: Toronto residents could face higher property taxes, TTC fares or service pressure in the next city budget if no new money arrives.
stories.now: Global News reports Ford shut the door on a new funding arrangement for Toronto on Wednesday, saying the province is in tough times. The comments follow the original three-year, $1.2-billion "New Deal" struck in November 2023 soon after Olivia Chow became mayor. CTV reports the city puts its 2027 budget gap at roughly $1.1 billion, and the 2023 deal, which provided about $1.2 billion over three years, expires this year.

stories.headline: U of T dentistry dean resigns after investigation into antisemitic course material
stories.summary: The University of Toronto says its dean of dentistry is stepping down immediately following an investigation into his use of antisemitic imagery in February.
stories.now: The University of Toronto announced Friday that the dean of its Faculty of Dentistry is leaving his post with immediate effect. The move follows an investigation into the dean's use of antisemitic imagery in course material in February. Details of the investigation's findings and who will lead the faculty on an interim basis were not in the reports available at publication time.
stories.backstory: The imagery surfaced in February and prompted complaints and a university review. The case adds to ongoing debate on Canadian campuses about antisemitism and how universities respond to complaints.

stories.headline: 'Message to the West' bomb threats target European newsrooms and travel
stories.summary: Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received bomb threats from someone using the name 'Mikhail Andropov'; live reports describe a wider wave of hoax threats across Europe.
stories.now: Al Jazeera reports newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received bomb threats signed by a person calling themselves 'Mikhail Andropov', under the banner 'Message to the West'. The Guardian's live coverage describes a high alert over hoax threats touching France, Belgium and air travel. Authorities have not publicly said who is behind the threats, and the reports describe them as hoaxes.
stories.backstory: Hoax bomb threats are a recurring tactic used to disrupt media outlets and transport and to stir public anxiety. European governments have warned of hybrid campaigns during the Ukraine war, though no link has been confirmed here.

stories.why: Repeated threats can disrupt flights, newsrooms and public events even when no device exists, and officials are watching for a coordinated source.
stories.impact: Travellers from Toronto to Europe could see delays if airports or airlines react to threats; check flight status before heading out.
